title: Judge Reformers by what they teach ex professo, not by strained inferences
source_text: CXXVII. Judicandum etiam lectoribus relinquo, quam vana sit viri Docti gloriatio, qua jactat se non timere, ut ullus Reformatorum audeat ipsum accusare, quod quicquam iis imponat, dum intrepide asserit, ex communi eorum sensu, proprium & formalem actum fidei justificantis esse certam fiduciam de obtenta a Deo remissione peccatorum? & praeterea annon aequius sit de Reformatorum sententia judicare, ex illis quae ipsi diserte docent & affirmant, dum ex professo tractant hanc Quaestionem, quam ex consequentis aliunde petitis, quales sunt eae quibus plurimum utitur vir Doctus, quicum jam mihi res est, ut probet eam esse communiter receptam Scholae Reformatae doctrinam, quam a plurimis ejus Doctoribus expresse tamen rejici ostendimus.
pass_a_gloss: I also leave readers to judge how vain is the Learned Man's boasting when he boasts he does not fear that any of the Reformers would dare accuse him of imposing anything on them, while he boldly asserts that from their common sense the proper and formal act of justifying faith is certain trust concerning remission of sins obtained from God? And further, whether it is not fairer to judge of the Reformers' opinion from those things they clearly teach and affirm when they treat this Question ex professo, than from consequences drawn from elsewhere — such as those the Learned Man with whom I now deal chiefly uses to prove that to be the commonly received doctrine of the Reformed School which we have shown is nonetheless expressly rejected by very many of its Doctors.
pass_b_english: The opponent boasts no Reformer would accuse him of misrepresentation while claiming their common sense makes obtained-remission trust faith's formal act.
Better to judge Reformers by what they teach when they treat this question head-on than by strained side-inferences — especially when many doctors expressly reject his 'common' doctrine.
